✧ Variant. Who killed Goliath? 2 Sam 21:19 says Elhanan killed Goliath the Gittite, in flat contradiction with 1 Sam 17 (David and Goliath). 1 Chr 20:5, telling the same story as 2 Sam 21:19, harmonizes by reading "Elhanan… killed Lahmi the brother of Goliath." Most modern textual critics (e.g., McCarter, Anchor Bible) treat the Chronicler’s text as a deliberate harmonization and 2 Sam 21:19 as preserving an older tradition in which Elhanan was the original Goliath-slayer; the David-Goliath story of 1 Sam 17 is then read as a transferred or composite tradition. The traditional alternative — that two different giants happened to share the name — is defensible but less economical. The verse is one of the textbook cases where two biblical narratives cannot both be straightforwardly historical without harmonization.

◇ Note. The Moabite execution policy. David’s treatment of Moab — making prisoners lie on the ground and killing two-thirds of them by measured line — is one of the harshest acts attributed to him. The brutality sits awkwardly alongside David’s Moabite ancestry: his great-grandmother Ruth was Moabite (Ruth 4:13–22), and during Saul’s persecution David sheltered his parents with the Moabite king (1 Sam 22:3–4). Some scholars (so McCarter) read the policy as personal revenge for a betrayal at that earlier sheltering, since 1 Sam 22 mentions David’s parents but doesn’t bring them home. The narrative offers no theological commentary, but its placement in the conquest summary registers Moab’s subjugation as a turning point — by the time of Mesha’s ninth-century revolt (the Moabite Stone, 2 Kgs 3), Israel’s domination of Moab is the political baseline that revolt is against.

◇ Note. Joab’s pre-battle speech. Joab’s exhortation closes with theological poise rare in his portrayal: "may Yahweh do what seems good to him." The phrase concedes the outcome to Yahweh while still demanding human effort — a posture summarizing the OT theology of holy war (cf. Deut 20:1–4, the priest’s pre-battle address). Joab is usually shown as a calculator and assassin; here, briefly, he speaks like Israel’s tradition speaks. The speech echoes Moses’ charge to Joshua (Deut 31:6, "be strong and of good courage") and is itself echoed in Paul’s charge to the Corinthians (1 Cor 16:13). Even the most morally compromised characters can voice the tradition’s best language; the book of Samuel takes its complicated figures seriously enough to let them.

◇ Note. David’s silence. The MT says only that David was "very angry"; the LXX and 4QSamᵃ preserve a longer reading: "but he would not punish his son Amnon, because he loved him, since he was his firstborn." Most modern translations (NRSV, NABRE) restore the longer reading, which makes explicit what the MT only implies — David’s rage produces no action. The vacuum is what Absalom fills: two years later (13:23) he kills Amnon himself, and the failure of paternal justice becomes the seed of the rebellion. The verse is one of the sharpest places where the David narrative exposes the cost of his moral compromise after the Bathsheba affair: the king who once executed king-killers swiftly (1:15, 4:12) cannot now bring himself to act against his own son. Robert Alter reads it as the narrative’s anatomy of Davidic paralysis.

◇ Note. Absalom’s hair. Two hundred shekels is roughly five pounds — implausible as the literal weight of any cut of human hair, almost certainly a hyperbolic detail meant to mark Absalom as exceptionally beautiful (the chapter has just told us, 14:25, that "from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him"). The narrative will return to that hair in 18:9, where Absalom’s head is caught in the branches of an oak as he flees the battle, leaving him hanging while his mule rides on. The most-prized feature becomes the instrument of his death — a deliberate literary closure of the kind Hebrew narrative reserves for figures whose vanity defines them. The text invites no allegory but builds the link unmistakably: what made Absalom dangerous is what kills him.

◇ Note. Ittai’s oath. Ittai the Gittite — a Philistine mercenary commander who arrived in David’s service only "yesterday" (15:20) — pledges loyalty to the fleeing king with language that consciously echoes Ruth’s oath to Naomi (Ruth 1:16–17). The two passages are the OT’s great covenantal oaths spoken by foreigners to Israelites at moments of catastrophe, and both reverse the usual direction of fidelity: the outsider out-loyals the insider. Ittai is one of three Gathite commanders David trusts (cf. 18:2), and the inclusion of a Philistine — historically the archetypal enemy of Israel — at the head of David’s troops in his hour of crisis is part of the chapter’s argument: those who follow David in his weakness are not necessarily those who would have followed him in his strength.

◇ Note. The prayer that the narrative answers. David’s short prayer here is precisely fulfilled in 17:14: "Yahweh had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel." Few biblical prayers are answered with such structural exactness — the request is granted, by name, two chapters later. The narrative pattern instructs the reader on how the book’s providence works: Yahweh acts through Hushai’s rhetorical skill and Absalom’s political vanity rather than by miracle, but the connection between the petition and its answer is unmistakable. Compare the way Hannah’s prayer (1 Sam 1:11) and Solomon’s (1 Kgs 3:9) operate in the same narrative-providence mode — explicit request, deferred and indirect fulfillment, narrator’s comment confirming the linkage. The books of Samuel teach the reader to recognize these arcs.

◇ Note. The cherub-throne theophany. The image — Yahweh riding on a cherub, flying on the wings of the wind — draws on ANE storm-god iconography, particularly the Canaanite Baal-Hadad, who likewise rides clouds and storms. The same imagery underlies Ps 18:10 (the parallel preservation of this poem) and is developed dramatically in Ezek 1 and 10 (the cherub-throne chariot of the divine glory). The cherubim themselves are not the chubby winged children of post-Renaissance art but composite guardian-creatures of the ANE imagination — winged, lion-or-bull-bodied, often human-faced (the Akkadian kāribu). The verse is one of the OT’s clearest cases of the inspired writer absorbing imagery from surrounding cultures and re-deploying it: the storm-god vocabulary is now spoken of Yahweh, the chariot-throne is now Yahweh’s, the foreign visual world has been theologically annexed.

⌘ Hebrew. Ḥasid (חָסִיד). "With the merciful you will show yourself merciful" — the Hebrew root is ḥesed, the same word that runs through ch 9 (David’s kindness to Mephibosheth). The ḥasid is one bound by covenant loyalty, the human partner who returns Yahweh’s ḥesed with reciprocal faithfulness. The word later becomes the name of a Jewish religious movement (the Ḥasidim of the Maccabean era, then the Ḥasidic Judaism of the eighteenth century). The verse opens a four-fold meditation (22:26–27) on the principle that Yahweh’s response mirrors human disposition — a theology developed in Ps 18:25–26 (the parallel) and quietly contested by Job, who finds it inadequate to his case. The verse is both a confession and a question.

And in the top of the base [was there] a round compass of half a cubit high: and on the top of the base the ledges thereof and the borders thereof [were] of the same.

↩

The First Book of Kings 7:36.

For on the plates of the ledges thereof, and on the borders thereof, he graved cherubims, lions, and palm trees, according to the proportion of every one, and additions round about.

↩

The First Book of Kings 7:37.

After this [manner] he made the ten bases: all of them had one casting, one measure, [and] one size.

↩

The First Book of Kings 7:38.

¶ Then made he ten lavers of brass: one laver contained forty baths: [and] every laver was four cubits: [and] upon every one of the ten bases one laver.

↩

The First Book of Kings 7:39.

And he put five bases on the right side of the house, and five on the left side of the house: and he set the sea on the right side of the house eastward over against the south.

↩

The First Book of Kings 7:40.

¶ And Hiram made the lavers, and the shovels, and the basons. So Hiram made an end of doing all the work that he made king Solomon for the house of the LORD:

↩

The First Book of Kings 7:41.

The two pillars, and the [two] bowls of the chapiters that [were] on the top of the two pillars; and the two networks, to cover the two bowls of the chapiters which [were] upon the top of the pillars;

↩

The First Book of Kings 7:42.

And four hundred pomegranates for the two networks, [even] two rows of pomegranates for one network, to cover the two bowls of the chapiters that [were] upon the pillars;

↩

The First Book of Kings 7:43.

And the ten bases, and ten lavers on the bases;

↩

The First Book of Kings 7:44.

And one sea, and twelve oxen under the sea;

↩

The First Book of Kings 7:45.

And the pots, and the shovels, and the basons: and all these vessels, which Hiram made to king Solomon for the house of the LORD, [were of] bright brass.

↩

The First Book of Kings 7:46.

In the plain of Jordan did the king cast them, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarthan.

↩

The First Book of Kings 7:47.

And Solomon left all the vessels [unweighed], because they were exceeding many: neither was the weight of the brass found out.

↩

The First Book of Kings 7:48.

And Solomon made all the vessels that [pertained] unto the house of the LORD: the altar of gold, and the table of gold, whereupon the shewbread [was],

↩

The First Book of Kings 7:49.

And the candlesticks of pure gold, five on the right [side], and five on the left, before the oracle, with the flowers, and the lamps, and the tongs [of] gold,

↩

The First Book of Kings 7:50.

And the bowls, and the snuffers, and the basons, and the spoons, and the censers [of] pure gold; and the hinges [of] gold, [both] for the doors of the inner house, the most holy [place, and] for the doors of the house, [to wit], of the temple.

↩

The First Book of Kings 7:51.

So was ended all the work that king Solomon made for the house of the LORD. And Solomon brought in the things which David his father had dedicated; [even] the silver, and the gold, and the vessels, did he put among the treasures of the house of the LORD.
